title: Adapt
hook: The pager log can name the engineer and still miss the system that set him up.
counterintuition: The visible bug gets the credit, but the deeper cause is often the system that made the bug likely. Adapt by fixing that cause without burying speed.
tryThisNow: Pick one recurring problem and ask why five times on paper. Stop only when the answer names a system, handoff, rule, or training gap you can change.
keyTakeaway: Use feedback loops and Five Whys to fix the system behind repeat failures without turning every next move into paperwork.

breakdown.fastRead:
Lin sits with a frozen status page beside the pager log. The outage has a name attached, but the handoff chart shows three teams passing ownership in the same unclear place.

Root-cause work keeps the room from blaming the last person near the problem.

A quick fix can restore service and still leave the next outage half-built. Adaptation means tracing the recurring failure into the human system that keeps producing it. Then the team changes the handoff, checklist, training, or feedback loop without burying the whole organization in process.
breakdown.deepRead:
"The towels are not disappearing," Margaux says outside room 412, where the linen cart is stopped again. The housekeeping checklist says restock after inspection. The restock time overlaps with checkout rush, so rooms keep opening short.

The missing towel is the symptom.

Five Whys prevents the team from stopping at the first person who touched the problem. Adaptive work is not blame with better vocabulary. It asks why the same pattern returns and what part of the system makes it likely. A technical problem may start with a bug, a badge reader, a form, or an oven timer. The recurring cause often sits in ownership, timing, training, or handoff design.

This is why feedback loops matter. The organization needs a way for local pain to change the process without waiting for a crisis. Too little process means the same preventable errors return. Too much process means learning speed dies under approvals.

The fix should be just heavy enough to stop paying for the same failure.

In the next staff huddle, Margaux marks the linen-cart route on a floor map instead of naming the last person who opened room 412. The map shows why the shortage appears at checkout rush: inspection finishes before restock has a clear owner. One small handoff change solves more than another reminder. The team learns where the failure is manufactured.
breakdown.fullRead:
Anders stands between a fax tray overflowing with refill requests and an online queue full of duplicates. The clinic keeps apologizing for same-day stress. Each week, staff blame the latest rush. The ownership map shows the real shape: refill requests enter through three channels, and nobody owns the merge before noon.

He maps the human system before changing the software.

Recurring technical problems often trace back to human systems. A queue can be badly designed. A badge reader can be reset perfectly while onboarding leaves new staff confused. A registration form can be accurate in each field and still impossible for parents to follow. The visible incident is where the pain appears, not always where the cause lives.

Where does the mistake become likely before anyone makes it?

Sofia faces that at a youth soccer registration table. Envelopes are stacked in uneven piles, and the board wants to blame parents for incomplete forms. She asks why five times. Why are envelopes incomplete? The form sequence sends families from payment to medical release and back to team choice. Why does that matter? Volunteers answer questions in different order. By the end of the chain, the board can see its own form design creating the error.

Adaptation should make the next mistake less likely without turning every decision into paperwork. That is the balance. The wrong response to every error is another approval layer. The right response is a targeted system change that preserves learning speed. A new owner for a handoff. A clearer checklist at the point of use. A training step where the confusion actually starts.

Devon learns this with data-center badges. The reader blinks red at the glass door, and the incident log shows repeated lockouts after resets. The technical fix is easy: reset the badge. The adaptive fix changes the onboarding checklist so new staff learn the access sequence before the first night shift. The badge reader was not the root cause. The training gap was.

There is a reason teams avoid this work. Systems make everyone a little responsible, which is less satisfying than naming one culprit. But a culprit gives relief for a day. A system change gives the next person a better chance.

Giulia sees the small version in a bakery. A tray of dark rolls cools under the timer, and the handoff note does not mention yesterday's oven calibration mark. Before, the morning shift added a second approval after burned batches. After tracing the cause, she rewrites the handoff loop so calibration changes are marked beside the timer. No new committee. No heavy review. Just the missing feedback in the place where the next batch starts.

Adaptive organizations improve process and quality while keeping the work alive. They do not worship speed so much that mistakes repeat forever, and they do not worship control so much that learning stops moving.

examples.title: Lin Follows the Pager Log Past Blame

planSpec.stakes: quick fixes keep repeating because escalation ownership is unclear
planSpec.requiredBeat: Lin uses Five Whys until the outage points to handoff design, not one engineer

examples.scenario: At 11:40 a.m. Monday, Lin sits in the postmortem with the status page frozen beside the pager log. The first story blames one engineer for missing escalation. The handoff chart tells a wider story. Before the fix is assigned, Lin must choose between naming the person nearest the outage and using Five Whys until ownership design is visible. The handoff chart shows Lin where the outage is produced before another person is blamed.
examples.whatToDo: Run Five Whys past the first human error and map the handoff. Change escalation ownership where the outage became likely.
examples.whyItMatters: Quick fixes repeat when the system stays intact. The pager log names the incident, but the handoff chart shows why the next one is already waiting.

examples.title: Margaux Finds the Restock Timing Gap

planSpec.stakes: room defects recur because the checklist hides ownership gaps
planSpec.requiredBeat: Margaux traces repeated towel shortages to a restock timing system

examples.scenario: "The towels are missing before anyone owns them," Margaux says beside a linen cart stopped outside room 412. The checklist says restock after inspection, but restock time lands during checkout rush. Another complaint is open. The operations manager must choose between another reminder and tracing the shortage to the timing system. The linen route lets Margaux fix the ownership gap instead of scolding the last housekeeper.
examples.whatToDo: Move the towel restock owner and time before the checkout rush. Fix the checklist where the shortage is created, not where guests report it.
examples.whyItMatters: Repeated room defects are not always carelessness. The checklist can hide the ownership gap that keeps producing the same shortage.

examples.title: Anders Maps the Refill Queue

planSpec.stakes: same-day stress returns because requests enter through three channels
planSpec.requiredBeat: Anders maps the human system behind recurring refill errors

examples.scenario: The fax tray overflows beside the online queue while Anders counts duplicate refill requests. Same-day stress has returned for the third Thursday in a row. The ownership map is blank at noon. He has a decision to make: clear today's queue again, or map the human system where three channels become one unmanaged pile. The fax tray and online queue show Anders that channel merge ownership is the real clinic failure.
examples.whatToDo: Map who owns each refill channel and the noon merge. Change the ownership point before adding another reminder to work faster.
examples.whyItMatters: The queue will keep failing if requests enter through three doors with no owner. Mapping the human system finds the cause before the next rush.

examples.title: Sofia Asks Why Until the Form Confesses

planSpec.stakes: blaming parents masks a confusing form sequence
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sofia asks why five times until the board sees its own form design

examples.scenario: You are beside Sofia at a folding table covered in registration envelopes and half-finished forms. The board is ready to blame parents again. Sofia starts a question chain on the back of one envelope. Before the next registration night, she needs to decide whether to send another scolding email or ask why until the form sequence is exposed. The envelope piles help Sofia trace incomplete forms to sequence and volunteer guidance.
examples.whatToDo: Ask why five times, then rewrite the form sequence where parents get lost. Fix the design before blaming families for predictable errors.
examples.whyItMatters: Incomplete envelopes look like parent carelessness. The question chain can reveal that the board built confusion into the registration flow.

examples.title: Devon Changes the Badge Onboarding

planSpec.stakes: technical badge resets miss the training gap causing repeated lockouts
planSpec.requiredBeat: Devon changes the onboarding system rather than the badge reader alone

examples.scenario: Giulia pulls a tray of dark rolls from under the oven timer at 4:25 a.m. in the bakery prep room while yesterday's calibration mark sits only in someone's memory. As shift lead, she sees the handoff note has no place for oven changes. In the postmortem, she must decide whether to add another approval or rewrite the handoff loop beside the timer. The timer note gives Giulia a local feedback loop instead of another slow approval layer.
examples.whatToDo: Add the access sequence to onboarding and verify it before night shifts. Keep badge resets, but treat them as symptoms until training changes.
examples.whyItMatters: A technical reset can solve today and miss tomorrow. The repeated lockout comes from a human-system gap, not the reader alone.

examples.title: Giulia Rewrites the Oven Handoff

planSpec.stakes: burned batches continue because shift notes omit oven calibration changes
planSpec.requiredBeat: Giulia rewrites the handoff loop without adding a heavy approval process

examples.scenario: At 4:25 a.m. in the bakery prep room, Devon stands beside a tray of dark rolls cooling under the oven timer while the calibration mark sits only in someone's memory. As shift lead, he sees why the morning crew added a second approval after burned batches. After tracing the cause, he rewrites the handoff loop so calibration changes are marked beside the timer. The badge log shows Devon where onboarding fails before the next night shift begins.
examples.whatToDo: Move the calibration mark into the handoff note beside the timer. Fix the feedback loop at the shift change instead of adding heavy review.
examples.whyItMatters: Burned batches keep returning when the next shift cannot see what changed. A targeted handoff fix preserves speed while reducing repeat errors.

questions.prompt: A hotel keeps opening rooms without enough towels, and the manager wants to blame whichever housekeeper touched the room last. The linen cart route and checkout rush show the problem repeats at the same handoff. What should the team inspect first?
choices: Which human system makes the failure likely before the engineer touches it?
Which engineer needs stricter punishment?
How can the team add approvals to every future deployment?
questions.explanation: Adaptation traces repeat failures into the system that produces them. Blame and blanket approvals may feel decisive while leaving the cause untouched or slowing learning.

questions.prompt: A hotel keeps finding rooms short on towels. The checklist assigns restock after inspection, during checkout rush. What should the manager change?
choices: Send a stronger reminder to all housekeepers.
Move ownership and timing for restock before the rush.
Require a manager signature on every room inspection.
questions.explanation: The recurring cause is timing and ownership, not likely memory. A targeted change beats another reminder or heavy approval layer.

questions.prompt: A clinic has duplicate refill requests because fax, portal, and phone requests merge late. Which move best fits adaptation?
choices: Tell patients to stop using fax immediately.
Ask staff to clear the queue faster each afternoon.
Map channel ownership and assign the merge point before noon.
questions.explanation: The ownership map changes the system producing duplicates. Banning one channel or working faster may not fix the recurring merge failure.

questions.prompt: A volunteer board blames parents for incomplete forms, but the form sequence sends families in circles. What should happen next?
choices: Ask why repeatedly until the form design behind the errors is visible.
Charge a fee for every incomplete envelope.
Add a second signature line to prove parents read the form.
questions.explanation: Five Whys can reveal the design problem before the board punishes families. Fees and signatures add friction without fixing the confusing sequence.

questions.prompt: A data center keeps resetting badges after lockouts, but new night staff keep getting stuck. Which fix addresses the likely root cause?
choices: Replace all badge readers immediately.
Add access-sequence practice to onboarding.
Tell night staff to arrive earlier.
questions.explanation: The repeated pattern points to training, not only hardware. Onboarding practice changes the system that creates the lockout.

questions.prompt: A bakery adds approvals after burned batches, but the calibration note still disappears between shifts. What is wrong with the response?
choices: It refuses to take quality seriously enough.
It should replace all oven timers before reviewing handoffs.
It adds process without fixing the feedback loop where the error begins.
questions.explanation: The approval layer slows work while the missing calibration handoff remains. Adaptation should target the cause and preserve learning speed.

questions.prompt: A bakery adds a second approval after burned rolls, but the oven calibration note still never reaches the morning shift. What makes the approval layer a weak adaptive response?
choices: Keep asking why until the answer names a system, handoff, training, or process condition.
Accept the answer because a person has finally been identified.
Move to punishment so everyone remembers next time.
questions.explanation: Stopping at the first person leaves the system intact. The method should reveal why forgetting was likely or unprotected.

questions.prompt: After each defect, a company adds another required approval. Defects fall slightly, but release learning slows badly. What is the adaptive concern?
choices: The company should never add process after defects.
The company may be improving quality by killing the feedback speed it needs.
The company should ignore defects until customers complain.
questions.explanation: Adaptive systems improve quality without freezing learning. Some process may help, but blanket approvals can overshoot the cause.

questions.prompt: A recurring technical failure traces to unclear ownership between two teams. Which response best balances quality and speed?
choices: Require executive approval for every handoff.
Keep the current process and ask both teams to be more careful.
Clarify the handoff owner and add a local feedback check at that point.
questions.explanation: A local ownership fix targets the recurring cause without slowing every decision. Executive approval is too broad, and care reminders preserve the defect.

reviewCards.front: A postmortem stops at the person who touched the failure last. What is Five Whys trying to prevent?
reviewCards.back: It prevents the team from stopping at the visible incident or nearest person. The aim is to find the system condition that makes repeat failure likely.

reviewCards.front: A team adds approval after every defect and delivery slows. Why can adding process after every mistake be harmful?
reviewCards.back: It can slow learning without fixing the cause. Adaptive process should target the system gap that produced the repeat failure.

reviewCards.front: A technical problem keeps returning. What nontechnical places should you inspect?
reviewCards.back: Inspect handoffs, ownership, training, timing, incentives, and feedback loops. The technical trigger may be downstream of a human system.

reviewCards.front: How does an adaptive organization protect speed?
reviewCards.back: It makes targeted system changes instead of adding broad approvals. The fix should reduce repeat failure while keeping learning moving.

reviewCards.front: A postmortem ends with a changed handoff instead of another reminder. What is the sign that it found a real root cause?
reviewCards.back: The proposed change makes the next similar failure less likely at the point where it becomes likely, not merely after damage appears.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to adapt without smothering learning. The skill is tracing repeated failure into the human system, then changing the smallest process point that prevents recurrence.

ifThenPlans.plan: If the first cause names a person, then ask why again until a system condition appears.
If the same defect returns twice, then map timing and ownership before adding another checklist.
If a fix restores service, then ask what feedback loop would make the same issue visible earlier next time.
If a proposed fix adds approval, then verify it targets the root cause and does not slow unrelated learning.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tomorrow, pick one repeat annoyance and run a written Five Whys chain until the answer names a handoff, ownership, training, or timing change.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one recurring failure. Replace one reminder or broad approval with a targeted system change and check whether the next occurrence becomes less likely.

memorableLines.text: Five Whys prevents the team from stopping at the first person who touched the problem.
memorableLines.why: It captures the source anchor and the anti-blame purpose in one sentence.

memorableLines.text: The missing towel is the symptom.
memorableLines.why: It teaches readers to look behind visible defects.

memorableLines.text: But a culprit gives relief for a day.
memorableLines.why: It contrasts blame with system repair in memorable form.
